{{Short description|Prime number with a certain relationship to an elliptic curve}}
In [[algebraic number theory]], a '''supersingular prime''' for a given [[elliptic curve]] is a [[prime number]] with a certain relationship to that curve. If the curve <math>E</math> is defined over the [[rational number]]s, then a prime <math>p</math> is '''supersingular for ''E''''' if the [[Good reduction#G|reduction]] of <math>E</math> modulo <math>p</math> is a [[supersingular elliptic curve]] over the [[residue field]] <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math>.{{sfn|Silverman|1986|pp=137–144}}

Equivalently, for a prime <math>p > 3</math> of [[good reduction]] for <math>E</math>, the prime is supersingular for <math>E</math> if and only if the [[Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves#Hasse–Weil Bound|trace of the Frobenius endomorphism]] <math>a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p)</math> is zero, that is, <math>\#E(\mathbb{F}_p) = p + 1</math>.{{sfn|Silverman|1986|pp=137–144}} This condition means that the reduction of <math>E</math> modulo <math>p</math> has the maximum possible [[endomorphism ring]]—an order in a [[quaternion algebra]]—rather than an order in an [[imaginary quadratic field]].{{sfn|Deuring|1941}}

== Distribution ==

=== Complex multiplication case ===

When <math>E</math> has [[complex multiplication]] (CM) by an order in an imaginary quadratic field <math>K</math>, the distribution of supersingular primes is well understood. A classical result of [[Max Deuring|Deuring]] (1941) implies that a prime <math>p</math> of good reduction is supersingular for <math>E</math> if and only if <math>p</math> is inert or ramified in <math>K</math>.{{sfn|Deuring|1941}} By the [[Chebotarev density theorem]], these primes constitute exactly half of all primes, so the set of supersingular primes for a CM curve has [[natural density]] <math>1/2</math>.{{sfn|Serre|1998|p=I-25}}

=== Non-CM case ===

When <math>E</math> does not have complex multiplication, the situation is more subtle. In 1968, [[Jean-Pierre Serre|Serre]] proved that the set of supersingular primes has [[natural density|asymptotic density]] zero by applying the [[Chebotarev density theorem]] to the number fields generated by coordinates of the [[torsion point|torsion points]] of <math>E</math>.{{sfn|Serre|1998|p=I-25}}{{sfn|Elkies|1991|p=127}} Serre later obtained the unconditional upper bound

:<math>\pi_{E,0}(x) \ll \frac{x}{\left(\log x\right)^{3/2 - \varepsilon}}</math>

for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, where <math>\pi_{E,0}(x)</math> denotes the number of supersingular primes up to <math>x</math>, and showed that under the [[Generalized Riemann Hypothesis]] (GRH) one could achieve the bound <math>\pi_{E,0}(x) \ll x^{3/4}</math>.{{sfn|Serre|1981|p=357}}{{sfn|Elkies|1991|p=127}} The unconditional exponent was subsequently improved by Wan (1990), who showed

:<math>\pi_{E,0}(x) \ll \frac{x}{\left(\log x\right)^{2 - \varepsilon}}</math>

by incorporating sieve-theoretic techniques.{{sfn|Wan|1990}}

Despite this rarity, [[Noam Elkies]] proved in 1987 that every elliptic curve over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> has infinitely many supersingular primes.{{sfn|Elkies|1987}} His proof uses the theory of [[complex multiplication]] and [[Deuring's lifting lemma]]: given any finite set <math>S</math> of primes, one can find a negative [[fundamental discriminant]] <math>-D</math> such that the [[Hilbert class polynomial]] <math>P_D(X)</math> evaluated at the [[j-invariant]] <math>j(E)</math> has a prime factor outside <math>S</math>, and this prime is necessarily supersingular for <math>E</math>.{{sfn|Elkies|1987}} Elkies later extended this result to elliptic curves defined over any [[number field]] with at least one [[real embedding]].{{sfn|Elkies|1989}}

=== Lang–Trotter conjecture ===

{{harvtxt|Lang|Trotter|1976}} conjectured that the number of supersingular primes less than a bound <math>X</math> satisfies

:<math>\pi_{E,0}(X) \sim C_E \frac{\sqrt{X}}{\log X}</math>

as <math>X \to \infty</math>, where <math>C_E > 0</math> is an explicit constant depending on <math>E</math>.{{sfn|Lang|Trotter|1976}} This prediction arises from a probabilistic heuristic: by the [[Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves|Hasse bound]], <math>|a_p| \leq 2\sqrt{p}</math>, so the "probability" that <math>a_p = 0</math> for a random prime <math>p</math> is roughly <math>1/\sqrt{p}</math>, and summing this over primes up to <math>X</math> gives an expected count on the order of <math>\sqrt{X}/\log X</math>.{{sfn|Lang|Trotter|1976}} {{as of|2026}}, this conjecture remains open.{{sfn|Cojocaru|Fouvry|Murty|2005}}

== Example ==

Consider the [[modular curve|elliptic curve]] <math>E : y^2 + y = x^3 - x^2 - 10x - 20</math>, which is the modular curve <math>X_0(11)</math> with [[j-invariant]] <math>j = -2^{12}/11</math>. The supersingular primes for this curve begin: 2, 19, 29, 199, 569, 809, 1289, 1439, 2539, 3319, ... {{OEIS|A006962}}.{{sfn|Elkies|1991|p=127}} These are exactly the primes <math>p</math> for which the coefficient of <math>q^p</math> in <math>\eta(\tau)^2 \eta(11\tau)^2</math> vanishes modulo <math>p</math>, where <math>\eta</math> is the [[Dedekind eta function]].

== Generalization ==

More generally, if <math>K</math> is any [[global field]]—that is, a [[finite extension]] of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> or of <math>\mathbb{F}_p(t)</math>—and <math>A</math> is an [[abelian variety]] defined over <math>K</math>, then a '''supersingular prime <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> for ''A''''' is a [[finite place]] of <math>K</math> such that the reduction of <math>A</math> modulo <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is a [[supersingular abelian variety]].{{sfn|Silverman|1986|pp=137–144}} It is conjectured that every abelian variety over a number field has infinitely many supersingular primes, but this is known only in special cases.{{sfn|Elkies|1989}}
